etymology: Hebrew miphqād, “an appointment,” “a mustering,” or “a census,” the gate of the appointed place, repaired by Malchiah over against the going up of the corner.
biblical_def: The gate Miphkad was one of the gates of Jerusalem set in order in the great day of the rebuilding of the wall, repaired by Malchiah the goldsmith’s son, who wrought unto the place of the Nethinims, and of the merchants, over against the gate Miphkad, and to the going up of the corner (Neh 3:31). The name signifies an appointment, a mustering, or a numbering, so that some have understood it the gate of the appointed place where the people were assembled and reviewed, or where judgment and account were rendered. It stood at the corner of the wall, near the close of the long circuit of builders that Nehemiah records, every man over against his own house. The dictionary marks it that the reader who walks the wall in the third chapter of Nehemiah may know it for a real gate in a real city, set in its appointed place. There is a quiet doctrine in the name, for the LORD is a God of appointment, who hath appointed a day in the which He will judge the world in righteousness, and who musters His people and numbers them as a shepherd telleth his sheep. The saint who passes the gate Miphkad may remember that there is an appointed reckoning, and so walk circumspectly, redeeming the time, as one who must give account.

etymology: Hebrew hānan’ēl, “God is gracious” or “whom God hath graced,” a fixed tower of the wall of Jerusalem, named in the rebuilding and in the promise of restoration.
biblical_def: The tower of Hananeel was a fixed and famous landmark of the wall of Jerusalem, standing toward the sheep gate at the north of the city. In the day of the rebuilding, Eliashib the high priest and his brethren the priests builded the sheep gate and sanctified it, even unto the tower of Meah they sanctified it, unto the tower of Hananeel (Neh 3:1); and when the companies of them that gave thanks went upon the wall, their circuit passed by the tower of Hananeel and the tower of Meah, even unto the sheep gate (Neh 12:39). More than a stone of the present wall, it was a fixed point of the promise, for the LORD spake by Jeremiah, Behold, the days come, that the city shall be built to the LORD from the tower of Hananeel unto the gate of the corner (Jer 31:38); and Zechariah set it as a bound of the restored and exalted Zion, from the tower of Hananeel unto the king’s winepresses (Zec 14:10). The name signifies “God is gracious,” and it is a gracious thing that the LORD should fix His city by such a tower. The dictionary honours that the watchtower of grace is set as a mark of both the rebuilding and the everlasting purpose of God, who is the keeper of the city, and without whom the watchman waketh but in vain.

etymology: Hebrew hammē’āh, “the hundred,” the tower of the hundred, a tower of the wall of Jerusalem sanctified together with the sheep gate and the tower of Hananeel.
biblical_def: The tower of Meah, which is the tower of the hundred, was a tower of the wall of Jerusalem standing toward the sheep gate, hard by the tower of Hananeel. In the day of the rebuilding, when Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brethren the priests and builded the sheep gate, they sanctified it even unto the tower of Meah, unto the tower of Hananeel (Neh 3:1); and when the companies of them that gave thanks went upon the wall, their circuit passed the tower of Hananeel and the tower of Meah, even unto the sheep gate (Neh 12:39). The name signifies “the hundred,” whence some have thought it a hundred cubits in height, or a hundred steps to its top, or that a hundred men of the guard kept watch upon it; but the Scripture leaves the reason in silence and only fixes the place. The dictionary marks it that the two towers stand together, sanctified by priestly hands, near the gate by which the sheep for sacrifice were brought into the city. There is a fitness in it, that the towers of watch should rise nearest the sheep gate, for the LORD keepeth His flock by setting watchmen upon the walls; and the believer is reminded that the city of God is both a fold for the sheep and a fortress with towers, where the great Shepherd is Himself the keeper of Israel that neither slumbers nor sleeps.

etymology: From the English of the KJV, the upper pool, Hebrew hab’rēkāh hā’elyōnāh, a reservoir of Jerusalem by whose conduit, in the highway of the fuller’s field, the great matters of Ahaz and Hezekiah were transacted.
biblical_def: The upper pool was a reservoir of Jerusalem, and the conduit that led from it ran along the highway of the fuller’s field, a place that the Scripture marks for two solemn meetings. There it was that the LORD bade Isaiah go forth to meet Ahaz, thou, and Shearjashub thy son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller’s field (Isa 7:3), and there the prophet pressed upon the trembling and unbelieving king the sign of the virgin’s Son, Immanuel, God with us. And there in the days of Hezekiah, the better king, Rabshakeh the railing servant of Assyria stood by the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller’s field, and lifted up his blaspheming voice against the living God and against the people of His trust (2Ki 18:17; Isa 36:2). One spot of water and dust, and two kings, the one unbelieving and the other believing, are set before us, and the difference of faith is made plain. The dictionary honours that the upper pool is a witness to the word of the LORD, spoken there in promise and assailed there in pride. The believer learns by it that the same place may prove the throne of unbelief or the altar of faith, according as men hear the word of God; and that He who is Immanuel is mighty to save them that trust in Him, and to bring to nought the boasting of the proud.

etymology: From the English of the KJV, the lower pool, Hebrew hab’rēkāh hattahtōnāh, a reservoir of Jerusalem to which the waters of the city were gathered in the day of trouble.
biblical_def: The lower pool was a reservoir of Jerusalem, named by Isaiah in his burden of the valley of vision, where he set before the city its frantic preparations in the day of the LORD’s controversy. Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many, said the prophet, and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool (Isa 22:9). When the enemy drew near, the men of Judah counted the houses and brake down the houses to fortify the wall, numbered their weapons in the house of the forest, and gathered the waters into the pools, that the city might endure the siege. All this was wisdom of a sort, for a besieged city must have water; yet the prophet’s charge was not against the gathering of the waters but against the heart that gathered them, for they looked to the cisterns and forgat the fountain, busied themselves with the stones and the streams but had not looked unto the maker thereof (Isa 22:11). The dictionary honours that the lower pool stands as a witness against the religion of the besieged that trusts in its own works of defence. The believer is warned by it that all our gathering of waters, all our shoring of walls, is vanity if we look not unto the maker thereof; for vain is the help of man, and except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.

etymology: From the English of the KJV, the old pool, Hebrew hab’rēkāh hayy’shānāh, an ancient reservoir of Jerusalem whose waters the men of Judah trusted, but looked not unto the maker thereof.
biblical_def: The old pool was an ancient reservoir of Jerusalem, named by Isaiah in his burden of the valley of vision among the works the city wrought in the day of her trouble. Ye made also a ditch between the two walls for the water of the old pool: but ye have not looked unto the maker thereof, neither had respect unto him that fashioned it long ago (Isa 22:11). When the siege drew near, the men of Judah laboured well by the rule of men, digging a ditch between the two walls that the water of the old pool might be secured to the city; and the work was not foolish, for water is the life of a besieged people. Yet the LORD’s controversy was with their hearts, for in all their digging and their walling they had not looked unto the maker thereof, neither had respect unto Him that fashioned it long ago. They trusted the old pool and the ancient ditch, the works of their own and their fathers’ hands, and forgat the everlasting God who fashioned the city and the very waters they gathered. The dictionary honours that the old pool, ancient as it was, could not save a people that looked not above it. The believer is taught that age and custom and the labour of the fathers are no refuge if the heart looks not unto the maker; for only the name of the LORD is a strong tower.

etymology: From the English of the KJV, the king’s pool, Hebrew b’rēkat hammelek, a reservoir of Jerusalem by the fountain gate, to which Nehemiah came in his night survey of the broken wall.
biblical_def: The king’s pool was a reservoir of Jerusalem, lying by the gate of the fountain at the south of the city, and it is named in the account of Nehemiah’s secret survey of the ruined wall. Having come to Jerusalem with a charge from God upon his heart, Nehemiah arose in the night, he and a few men with him, and told no man what God had put in his heart to do; and he went out by night by the gate of the valley, and viewed the walls of Jerusalem which were broken down, and the gates thereof consumed with fire. Then I went on to the gate of the fountain, and to the king’s pool: but there was no place for the beast that was under me to pass (Neh 2:14), so heaped were the ruins that even his beast could not go forward. The king’s pool thus marks the turning of his solemn circuit, where the rubble shut up the way. The dictionary honours that the work of restoration began with this quiet, prayerful, nighttime reckoning of the breaches, before ever a stone was laid. The believer learns from the king’s pool that they who would build for God must first count the ruin honestly and in secret before Him, and that the LORD prospers the hand that surveys the breach upon its knees; for He who set His servant to view the broken wall was Himself the keeper of the city.

etymology: From the English of the KJV, “the pool that was made,” Hebrew hab’rēkāh hā’asūyāh, an artificial reservoir of Jerusalem by the king’s garden, near the wall of the pool of Siloah.
biblical_def: “The pool that was made” was an artificial reservoir of Jerusalem, a work of men’s hands gathered to hold the waters of the city, and it is named among the works of the rebuilt wall. After him repaired Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, the ruler of the half part of Bethzur, unto the place over against the sepulchres of David, and to the pool that was made, and unto the house of the mighty (Neh 3:16). It lay toward the king’s garden, near the wall of the pool of Siloah, where the conduit that Hezekiah made of old brought the water of Gihon down into the city; and it is likely the same artificial work as the ditch made between the two walls for the water of the old pool, whereof Isaiah spake (Isa 22:11). The dictionary marks that it is called expressly “the pool that was made,” a reservoir not of nature but of labour, the contrivance of men to hold the gift of God. There is a quiet lesson in the name, for the waters were the LORD’s, and only the pool was made of men; the streams that filled it were of His fountains, and the cistern only of their cutting. So the believer is reminded that even our best contrivances do but hold what God supplies, and that the maker of the waters is greater than the makers of the pool, who fashioned the springs of Jerusalem long ago.

corruption_paragraphs: “The pool that was made” is a feature of the sacred record of Nehemiah’s wall, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader who walks the wall may know it for a real reservoir in a real city, an artificial cistern by the king’s garden near the pool of Siloah.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the cistern is of men, but the waters are of God. The pool that was made was a work of human labour, yet it held only what the LORD’s fountains supplied; so it teaches that our best contrivances do but receive His gifts, and that the maker of the waters is far greater than the makers of the pool, who fashioned the springs of the city long ago.

etymology: Hebrew riblah, a city in the land of Hamath upon the Orontes, the northern headquarters of Pharaoh-nechoh and of Nebuchadnezzar, and the place where judgment fell upon faithless Judah.
biblical_def: Riblah was a city in the land of Hamath, set upon the great northern road, and it became the seat of judgment for two captains of the nations and two kings of Judah. There Pharaoh-nechoh of Egypt put Jehoahaz in bands, that he might not reign in Jerusalem, and laid the land under tribute (2Ki 23:33). And there the heavier stroke fell from the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, when Zedekiah, who had broken his covenant and rebelled, was overtaken in the plains of Jericho and brought up to Riblah, where they gave judgment upon him (2Ki 25:6; Jer 39:5). Then the king of Babylon slew the sons of Zedekiah in Riblah before his eyes, and afterward put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him with fetters of brass (2Ki 25:7); and there also the king of Babylon slew the princes and nobles of Judah (Jer 39:6; 52:10,27). Riblah is therefore a place of solemn and terrible justice, where the word of the LORD against the covenant-breaker was made good to the letter. The dictionary names plainly the judgment that fell there upon faithless Zedekiah, who despised the oath and lightly esteemed the word of the prophet. Let the reader tremble and learn, for the LORD is sovereign over the nations and over the thrones of kings, and judgment overtakes the man that breaks covenant with Him; yet to the penitent the same LORD is a strong tower, and the righteous that runneth into it is safe.

corruption_summary: A place where the LORD’s judgment fell upon the covenant-breaker; it witnesses that He is sovereign over the nations and that judgment overtakes the faithless king.
corruption_paragraphs: Riblah is a place of the sacred record, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader of the books of the kings and of Jeremiah may know it for a real city in the land of Hamath, the seat where the judgment of the LORD fell upon faithless Judah by the hand of Babylon.

Here the dictionary names the matter plainly, as the Scripture does. Zedekiah brake the oath he had sworn to the king of Babylon and despised the word of the LORD by the prophet Jeremiah; and at Riblah the covenant-breaker reaped what he had sown, seeing his sons slain before his eyes were put out. The principle to recover is that the LORD is sovereign over the nations and the thrones of kings, and that His judgment surely overtakes the man who breaks covenant with Him; yet the same LORD is a strong tower to the penitent, and the righteous that runneth into Him is safe.

etymology: Hebrew tsōbāh, Aram-zobah, a Syrian kingdom north of Damascus, the realm of Hadadezer the son of Rehob, whom Saul fought and David subdued.
biblical_def: Zobah, called also Aram-zobah, was a Syrian kingdom lying north of Damascus, a power of the heathen against which the kings of Israel waged war. Saul in his day fought against the kings of Zobah among all his enemies on every side, and whithersoever he turned himself he vexed them (1Sa 14:47). But it was David who broke their strength, for he smote Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates (2Sa 8:3), and took from him chariots and horsemen and footmen, and put garrisons among the Syrians of Damascus, so that the Syrians became servants to David and brought gifts; and the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went (2Sa 8:6). When the children of Ammon afterward hired the Syrians of Zoba against him, these too were beaten down (2Sa 10:6). David dedicated unto the LORD the silver and gold he won of Zobah, with the spoil of all the nations he subdued (2Sa 8:11-12); and the title of the sixtieth Psalm remembers his striving with Aram-zobah. The dictionary honours that here the LORD subdued the heathen under His anointed king, a figure of the greater Son of David who shall put all enemies under His feet. The believer is taught that through God we shall do valiantly, for He it is that shall tread down our enemies (Psa 60:12), and that every spoil of every victory belongs of right to the LORD.
